content.intro: In this lesson, you will study history and evolution of asp as part of Classic ASP development and legacy maintenance. The lesson follows the attached ASP curriculum topic 2 and uses the syllabus subtopics as the coverage checklist.
content.why_it_matters: History and Evolution of ASP matters because Classic ASP behavior crosses a server-side scripting engine, IIS configuration, request/response boundaries, and often COM or ADO dependencies. A small, explicit test helps distinguish intended behavior from runtime-specific behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Classic ASP is a server-side page technology: IIS processes an `.asp` request, executes server-side script, and returns the resulting response. For 'History and Evolution of ASP', keep a clear boundary between what runs on the server and what the browser receives. The curriculum places this topic in the foundations stage, so the aim is to recognize the role, context, and limits before building larger workflows.

content_blocks.title: Syllabus coverage
content_blocks.text: The lesson explicitly covers: Origins of Active Server Pages; Evolution of ASP and IIS; Relationship between Classic ASP and ASP.NET; Classic ASP in legacy enterprise applications. Treat these subtopics as connected requirements. For each one, be able to define the concept, identify where it appears in a Classic ASP application, and name one test or diagnostic that would verify it.

The source syllabus treats Classic ASP as a legacy maintenance technology, not as ASP.NET or a default choice for new web projects.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating legacy runtime behavior as universal.
common_mistakes.why: IIS versions, Windows lifecycle, COM registration/bitness, and ADO providers can change behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Write down the actual server/provider versions and validate on a disposable test site.

common_mistakes.why: Empty input, missing records, expired sessions, permissions, timeouts, and malformed data reveal different failure modes.
common_mistakes.fix: Add normal, negative, and boundary cases with expected outcomes.

common_mistakes.why: Detailed errors can reveal paths, SQL text, configuration, and component information.
common_mistakes.fix: Keep diagnostics in restricted server-side logs and return a generic message with a reference ID.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming syntax alone proves the application works.
common_mistakes.why: IIS configuration, permissions, COM activation, database providers, and response behavior are external dependencies.
common_mistakes.fix: Run against the documented local test host and record exact evidence.

common_mistakes.why: Query strings, form fields, cookies, and hidden controls remain client-controlled.
common_mistakes.fix: Validate on the server and apply authorization and output encoding at the appropriate boundary.
